definition: The practice of training a model across multiple GPUs, TPUs, or machines simultaneously to handle models or datasets too large for a single device.
details: Distributed training strategies include data parallelism (splitting the data across devices), model parallelism (splitting the model itself), and pipeline parallelism, often combined for training the largest LLMs.

explainer.lead: Distributed training spreads the work of training one model across several GPUs, TPUs, or machines. It makes training possible when the model or dataset is too large for a single device.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a school project too big for one desk, so several people work on it at their own desks. They can each take part of the materials, or each handle a different part of the project, to build one shared result.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers run training across multiple GPUs, TPUs, or machines when a single device cannot hold the workload. Data parallelism splits the data, model parallelism splits the model, and pipeline parallelism provides another way to divide the work; these strategies are often combined for the largest LLMs.
tiers.paperLevel: Given devices D = {d1, ..., dn}, distributed training performs one model-training workload across D rather than on a single device. Data parallelism partitions the training data across devices, while model parallelism partitions the model; pipeline parallelism is another strategy, and the approaches can be combined. Its scope is training models or datasets too large for one device, including the largest LLMs.

explainer.example: Suppose a training job uses four GPUs because its dataset is too large for one device. With data parallelism, each GPU receives a different quarter of the data; if the model itself also needs dividing, model or pipeline parallelism can be added.

usedIn.name: Large language model training
usedIn.detail: The largest LLMs often use combinations of data, model, and pipeline parallelism.

usedIn.name: Multi-GPU and TPU training
usedIn.detail: Training is spread across several accelerators when one device is insufficient.

usedIn.name: Multi-machine training
usedIn.detail: The workload can extend beyond one machine to handle very large models or datasets.

explainer.intuition: Instead of asking one device to hold and process everything, divide the training workload among many devices. The division can follow the data, the model, or pipeline stages.
howItWorks: Identify whether the dataset, the model, or both exceed a single device's capacity.
Connect multiple GPUs, TPUs, or machines for the training run.
Use data parallelism to give different devices different portions of the data.
Use model or pipeline parallelism when the model itself must be divided.
Combine strategies when training the largest LLMs.
explainer.whyItMatters: It expands training beyond the capacity of one device, allowing larger models and datasets to be handled. Combining parallelism strategies is especially important for the largest LLMs.
misconceptions: Distributed training does not always mean splitting the data; the model itself can also be split.
Data, model, and pipeline parallelism are not mutually exclusive and are often combined.
